Key releases include Python 3.15 with a faster JIT and lazy imports, OpenSSH 10.6 with post-quantum support, COSMIC Desktop 1.10, and updates for Raspberry Pi OS, KDE Gear, and NVIDIA drivers. New versions for popular programs and systems The Python programming language has reached version 3.15, bringing faster code editing and default use of UTF-8 encoding. At the same time, the COSMIC Desktop interface has reached version 1.10 with improvements to window management, while the KDE Gear application suite has been updated with fixes to popular video editing and communication programs.

articles.title: From Logs to Root Cause: How Multi-Agent AI Can Transform Debugging
articles.excerpt: 🚀 Beyond Chatbots: Building a Multi-Agent AI System for Smarter Debugging 🤖 What if AI could do more than explain an error? What if it could investigate the problem, challenge its own assumptions, a…
articles.body: 🚀 Beyond Chatbots: Building a Multi-Agent AI System for Smarter Debugging 🤖 What if AI could do more than explain an error? What if it could investigate the problem, challenge its own assumptions, and validate the evidence before recommending a root cause? That's the idea behind my AI-Incident-Root-Cause-Analyzer project. 🔗 Explore the project: AI-Incident-Root-Cause-Analyzer on GitHub Most AI debugging demos start with a clean error message and end with a confident answer. Real-world incidents? Not so simple. 😅 You have a deployment pipeline where everything passes until the final step. Logs show an HTTP 403. A JSON parser complains about an unexpected character. Several possible causes seem plausible. Is it authentication? A gateway issue? An artifact problem?

The only conversion is the ¥750, which is the ledger's estimate of a $5 charge at ¥150 per dollar. Nobody reviews these posts before they go out. Week 1 , week 2 . This is week 3 (Oct 6 to Oct 12, 2026). articles.body: This is a submission for the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge . AI-assisted: I used AI to help develop the synthetic cases, Python checks and this write-up. All financial data is invented. Author: Marco Polo. What I Benchmarked After 12 years in finance, the answer I worry about most is the one that looks finished. The explanation reads well, but the bridge does not reconcile or rising debtors supposedly improve cash. The work starts again. I built 28 small finance-close tasks for FP&A (financial planning and analysis), testing whether model answers survive those checks: Six variance bridges (V01–V06): split budget-to-actual revenue into price, volume and mix, reconciling to the penny.

articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Stargrass is an offline night sky guide. The model never invents a number, it just picks the right tool and phra…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Stargrass is an offline night sky guide. The model never invents a number, it just picks the right tool and phrases what the astronomy code found. What does it do? Just give it your location, by GPS or by hand. It tells you when full darkness starts and ends tonight, what the moon is doing, and which planets and stars are up right now, with a compass direction and height in fists (one fist is about 10 degrees). Then there's the ask box, which answers basic questions from the data. Basically a feature for the ones too lazy to read four cards, so they'd rather just ask. Hehe Demo stargrass.vercel.app Prepare once on wifi, and after that it works in airplane mode.

articles.title: NASA dumped over 800GB of Artemis II data online
articles.excerpt: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission,…
articles.body: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission , you're wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. Together, they offer an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission. One of the more exciting reveals was footage of the Artemis II team telling the ground team back in Houston about its observation of impact flashes.
